https://jowhar.com/is-russias-alleged-hy.text: Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim NEWS ARTICLE WORLD NEWS POLITICS Sport QURAN Video Somali TV privacy-policy terms and conditions Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim WORLD NEWS ARTICLE Facebook X Telegram WhatsApp ReddIt Pinterest Digg Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport on 4 August Germany’s relationship with Russia plunged to a fresh low this week after Berlin accused Moscow of playing a role in a drone attack targeting Leipzig-Halle Airport — an allegation the Kremlin rejects but one that has reignited fears across Europe of an expanding Russian “hybrid” campaign against countries backing Ukraine. The dispute, which Russia denies, has thrown a harsh spotlight on the growing debate over whether Europe is already facing a shadow conflict designed to intimidate, disrupt and divide EU states supporting Kyiv. Is this a genuine threat, and if so, what has been Europe’s response? The alleged hybrid pressure on Europe took a sharper turn when Germany formally blamed Russia for an attempted drone strike at Leipzig-Halle Airport on 4 August. “The means used,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt declared on Tuesday, “such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems, are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine”. Investigators say three drones were involved. One — packed with military grade explosives — was spotted by an alert bus driver beside a Ukrainian cargo plane. A second struck a cargo aircraft while it was in flight. A third, carrying traces of explosives, was later found in a nearby field. Germany moved quickly, ordering the immediate closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. Russian President Vladimir Putin, in turn, accused German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of trying to shift public attention ahead of this weekend’s pivotal regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the Russia-sympathetic AfD party is expected to triumph. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Berlin had produced no evidence and warned that Germany was “proceeding down a path of further escalation”. Yet on Wednesday, German media reported that police had identified two suspects through DNA traces: a Belarussian national holding a Russian passport and a joint Russian-Latvian national. Germany shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn in response to the incident in Leipzig What exactly is hybrid warfare? The episode — and the blunt exchanges between Berlin and Moscow — captures what officials and analysts describe as the essence of hybrid warfare: limited, often deniable actions calibrated to unsettle governments, strain alliances and keep rivals guessing about attribution and intent. Hybrid attacks have shadowed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine since 2022, but they are increasingly being described as cresting at a moment when Mr Putin, having failed to force a breakthrough on the battlefield and facing waning energy at home among the population and elites, is thought to be weighing escalation to break the impasse. “We will escalate our methods to destroy everything that helps Ukraine’s military coming from the West,” foreign minister Sergei Lavrov admitted recently. “In fact, we are already doing it.” What set Leipzig apart, German officials argue, was the recoverable hardware: unlike multiple drone sightings along Germany’s eastern flank last year, this custom-built quadcopter carried 600g of explosives — enabling authorities to dismantle and assess it. The central question now is whether Mr Putin is prepared to risk direct attacks — even indirect, hybrid ones such as sabotage and drone strikes — against NATO countries. Regardless of the answer, European capitals have struggled to assemble a response that is both unified and credible, a gap many believe the Kremlin is eager to exploit. Speaking on Wednesday at an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Druid’s Glen in Co Wicklow, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the Leipzig incidents bore “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”. Russia has denied any involvement in drone attacks on EU territory She added: “The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador.” Even after Berlin formally assigned responsibility to Russia, the immediate reaction fell short of what some observers anticipated. Chancellor Merz had telegraphed the accusation in advance, but said nothing publicly on the day, leaving the matter to the interior and foreign ministers and signalling that Germany would hold a tougher response in reserve should Russia strike again. “This is also an expression of the appropriateness of our reaction, ” foreign minister Johann Wadepuhl explained. “Germany can show a stronger reaction at any time.” What has Germany’s response been? After the Leipzig incidents, Minister Dobrindt doubled the number of specialist anti-drone police to 300, widened the areas in which they operate and announced a new drone research centre at Magdeburg-Cochsted Airport. Two weeks ago, Berlin introduced legislation aimed at a sweeping overhaul of the federal foreign and military intelligence service, the BND, explicitly to strengthen its ability to combat hybrid warfare. The political instinct, officials say, is to reach for more — and tougher — sanctions. Minister Wadepuhl said Germany would press for additional EU measures, including travel restrictions on Russian nationals, and intensify efforts against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers, long suspected of serving as seaborne launchpads for drones. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (L) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt held a press conference on Wednesday to address the incident But EU officials privately acknowledge that the bloc is approaching the limits of easy consensus: 21 sanctions packages are already in place, and further steps increasingly collide with national economic interests. Securing the 21st package in July, it is understood, proved particularly fraught. Athens objected to measures affecting Greek vessels that ship Russian LNG, while Austria pushed for Vienna-based Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) to access sanctioned assets linked to its Russian subsidiary to offset fines imposed by Moscow. “There’s a certain reflection going on in Brussels about whether it is really smart to continue doing this,” says one EU diplomat. “It’s getting more and more difficult and divisive. They are meant to be about holding Russia to account and eliminating its ability to wage war against Ukraine, when actually it’s dividing us.” Even so, officials widely expect the EU to proceed with a 22nd package. Have hybrid attacks been on the increase? Officials across the region say hybrid incidents are intensifying. On 26 August, Romanian F16 jets destroyed an explosive-laden drone loitering a few hundred metres from Netpun Deep — Europe’s largest natural gas platform — inside Romanian territorial waters. It was the fourth allegedly Russian drone shot down over Romania this year. Elsewhere, governments have reported an array of covert operations against states supporting Ukraine. On 16 November last, an explosion damaged the Warsaw to Lublin rail line used to move equipment to Kyiv — an attack Polish authorities blamed on two Ukrainian men allegedly working for the Russian foreign security service (FSB). Two months earlier, Lithuanian prosecutors said they had disrupted a Russian plan to send homemade incendiary devices through logistics companies including DHL, with one device exploding in Leipzig and another catching fire at a DHL hub in Birmingham. Intelligence services say dozens of other alleged drone and sabotage incidents have been recorded. A train from Warsaw to Lublin in Poland was damaged in an explosion last year blamed on men working for the Russian foreign security service Carnegie Europe, the international foreign and security policy think tank, says there have been 151 cases of sabotage and shadow warfare since 2022 either publicly attributed to Russia or suspected of involving Russia or Russia-adjacent actors. “Between 2023 and 2024, the number of such attacks quadrupled, and the tally for the following years continued on an upward curve. That is in addition to the daily informational warfare and intense political and election interference Europe is subjected to from various quarters,” says Carnegie’s Strategic Europe editor Rym Momtaz. The Institute for International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a July report that from August 2024 to February 2026, suspected Russian drones entered the airspace of a dozen NATO member states and Ireland, “forcing the closure of aviation hubs including Brussels, Copenhagen, Munich, Oslo and Vilnius”. The same report said drones disrupted smaller regional airports across Denmark, Germany and the Baltic states, and were spotted above European naval facilities and air bases — including locations hosting US nuclear weapons and a French ballistic missile submarine base. The IISS characterised the trend as a tactical win for the Kremlin and a strategic failure for Europe’s allied air defences. According to the report, the campaign seeks to “probing the response times and decision-making thresholds of allied air defence and civil-military command structures; mapping vulnerabilities around critical infrastructure, including dual-use civilian hubs, military logistics nodes supporting Ukraine, and facilities associated with allied nuclear deterrence; imposing economic and psychological costs on European societies through the disruption of civilian aviation and public confidence in airspace security”. The Danish prime minister said Russia’s involvement in drone sightings at Copenhagen Airport last year could not be ruled out More broadly, hybrid — or shadow — warfare is used as an umbrella term for relatively low-cost offensive tactics designed to weaken and confuse an opponent without crossing the line into open conflict. Those methods allegedly span election interference, online campaigns and other efforts aimed at stoking division, hostility and political fatigue. “Much like a hybrid vehicle, which seamlessly switches between gasoline and electricity without being noticed, hybrid warfare blends tools of statecraft and conflict,” said Eitvydas Bajarūnas, non-resident Senior Fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (CEPA). “Information manipulation campaigns segue into cyber attacks, which give way to political influence operations, economic pressure, or covert sabotage. The combination is designed to be adaptive, continuous, and hard to attribute, keeping the target off-balance.” Attribution remains difficult: identifying where drones come from is often complex, and Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement. Still, the IISS report argues that “the aggregate pattern of [drone] sightings cannot be adequately explained by misidentification, hobbyist activity or opportunistic harassment alone”. Danish authorities stopped short of definitive conclusions after drone incidents in September last year near Copenhagen airport and several military bases, but an earlier episode appeared more alarming. Up to 20 large drones were observed flying in formation over the Køge port before accelerating into the bay and vanishing at high speed. The port had previously served as Denmark’s main embarkation point for deployments to NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence in eastern Europe. How have sabotage operations worked? UK counter-terrorism police say Russia has relied on proxies to carry out attacks, adding another layer of deniability. Last October, Dylan Earl, 24, and Jake Reeves, 21, received a combined 29-year sentence for an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned business in east London in March 2024, which caused €1.16 million in damage. Two men, who police found were working for the Wagner Group, were found guilty of an arson attack on a Ukranian-owned business in London in 2024 (Photo: London Fire Brigade) Police said the pair made contact on Telegram with the Russian mercenary organisation, the Wagner Group, which paid them to carry out the arson and plan further attacks. Commander Dominic Murphy, head of the Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “This case is a clear example of an organisation linked to the Russian state using ‘proxies’ – in this case British men – to carry out very serious criminal activity in this country on their behalf.” Officials suspect other sabotage operations across Europe have similarly been executed by local proxies recruited via intermediaries. How long has Russia been operating a hybrid warfare doctrine? Analysts disagree on when the doctrine took shape. In 2019, Nicole Ng of Carnegie’s Russia and Eurasia Programme and Eugene Rumer, a former US national intelligence officer, traced the modern concept to 1996, when Yevgeny Primakov — then head of Russia’s foreign intelligence service — became foreign minister. After the Soviet Union’s collapse, Russia initially pursued accommodation with the West, but Primakov argued that a US-dominated unipolar world was unacceptable to Moscow. “He envisioned a multipolar world managed by a concert of major powers, with Russia as an indispensable actor with a vote and veto on key issues. “Securing Russia’s primacy in the post-Soviet space and opposing NATO enlargement were also crucial to Primakov’s vision.” That outlook aligned with Vladimir Putin’s instincts when the former Soviet intelligence officer who served in East Germany became Russia’s president in January 2000. In his 2007 speech at the Munich Security Conference, Mr Putin attacked the concept of a unipolar world, calling it not only unacceptable but “impossible in today’s world”. Russia invaded Georgia the following year. In February 2013, Russia’s chief of staff General Valery Gerasimov published a 2,000-word essay in a little-known military trade paper titled, “The Value of Science Is in the Foresight”. The article fused Soviet-era tactics with a modern theory of warfare aimed at weakening an adversary from within rather than relying on frontal assault. Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov presented a new theory of modern warfare “The very ‘rules of war’ have changed,” he wrote. “The role of non-military means of achieving political and strategic goals has grown, and, in many cases, they have exceeded the power of force of weapons in their effectiveness. “All this is supplemented by military means of a concealed character.” One year later, Russia invaded and annexed Crimea — an operation often described as hybrid because Mr Putin initially denied Russian troops were there, referring instead to “little green men”, before later acknowledging their presence after the campaign succeeded. Senior intelligence officials say they have no doubt Russia is waging a hybrid war against Europe. “We are in the middle of a hybrid war,” former vice-president of the German BND Ole Diehl told a German Council on Foreign Relations podcast. “Russia has not declared this war, but Russia is leading this war against us.The Russians say so quite clearly, they openly declare that there is no difference between a conventional military war, and a hybrid war. “Russia wants to destabilise our society, to stop our support for Ukraine, it wants to increase its influence not just in the former Soviet republics and Warsaw Pact countries, but also its influence on us, on Europe. “This hybrid war requires that we think differently about what the Russians are doing and what we are doing in response.” What is Europe doing in response? From the standpoint of those who deploy it, hybrid warfare has a built-in advantage: traditional defence and deterrence systems are often ill-suited or outdated for threats that sit below the threshold of open war. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/22/excl.text: Iran's new academic year opens on Wednesday against a backdrop of tuition fees that in some cases nearly tripled over the summer, with enrollment falling at private schools across Tehran as war fears, sanctions and the continued collapse of the rial squeeze family budgets.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian marked the start of the academic year by ringing the school bell at a girls' primary school in Tehran on Monday.The Ministry of Education has instructed schools to prioritise in-person teaching after periods of online learning during previous phases of the war.The ministry also issued a directive capping tuition increases at private schools at 35% for the new academic year, setting fees across the country at between 14 million and 145 million tomans (€53–€549). In practice, the cap is not being observed.Bita, a final-year high school student in eastern Tehran, told Euronews she paid 80 million tomans (€303) last year and 220 million tomans (€833) this year — a 175% increase."I'm in my final year of high school. Students in lower grades pay somewhat less. We also have to pay a separate fee for pamphlets and school-printed textbooks, which comes to around 20 million tomans (€76)," Bita said."Right now, for a senior at a private high school, their family has to pay roughly 250 million tomans (€947) for their education. Of course, in the affluent neighborhoods in the northern part of the city, this cost goes even higher," she explained.Although the rial is Iran’s official currency, everyday pricing and transactions are conducted in tomans — where 1 toman equals 10 rials — with the open market rate on Monday standing at slightly over 264,000 tomans (or 2,640,000 rials) per euro.Maryam, 57, works as an accountant at several private primary schools in southern Tehran.She said tuition at one school she works with rose from 36 million tomans (€136) two years ago to 85 million tomans (€322) this year. She has also seen declining enrolments driven not only by cost but by security concerns."At one of these schools many pupils have not enrolled because it is opposite a police station and their parents worry that if the war starts again their children will not be safe there," Maryam told Euronews."Their other concern is that classes may move online and they are not willing to pay heavy fees for virtual lessons at non-profit schools."One school in Tehran's Shahrak-e Valiasr district closed entirely after failing to reach the minimum enrolment required to operate, Maryam added.Luxury stationery bundlesOfficial statistics put total enrolment in Iran's fee-charging schools and universities at approximately 3.3 million students, of whom nearly 70% pay tuition.Total enrolment has fallen from 4.4 million students over the past decade, a decline the ministry partly attributes to reduced purchasing power.Mehra, a third-term law student at the Islamic Azad University in Tehran, said her combined fixed and variable tuition doubled from 11 million tomans (€41) to 22 million tomans (€83).The costs extend beyond tuition. A basic school supplies bundle now ranges from 3 million tomans (€11.30) to 17 million tomans (€64.30).A 500-sheet ream of CopyMax A4 paper — commonly used by university students for lecture notes — starts at 975,000 tomans (€3.69).Recycled newsprint A4 paper starts at 390,000 tomans (€1.48) but is considered unsuitable for school work. Prices also vary significantly depending on where in Tehran you buy supplies.Arya and his wife Roksana, who run a stationery shop in the small town of Vahidieh near Shahriar, on the outskirts of Karaj, told Euronews that although they source their stock from the same wholesale markets as sellers across Tehran and Karaj, they cannot match big-city prices.Arya said the price of a quality notebook rose from 85,000 tomans (€0.32) last year to 180,000 tomans (€0.68) this year, an increase of around 100%.Roksana said customer numbers had dropped but added that some families were simply using supplies left over from the previous year when many classes were held online and materials went largely unused."Our customer numbers have dropped, but that doesn't mean students aren't getting school supplies this year. For instance, my own son is using leftover notebooks from last year," Roksana told Euronews."Plus, with classes held online for much of the previous school year, students barely used their backpacks, shoes, and uniforms. As a result, families don't see the need to buy new ones this year," she concluded.

https://aa.com.tr/en/eurasia/russian-pre.text: Eurasia Russian presidential aide says Polish statehood could cease within days if Poland enters conflict with Russia Nikolay Patrushev responds to Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski's claim that Poland could defeat Russia quickly Elena Teslova 15 September 2026 • Update : 15 September 2026 MOSCOW Russian presidential aide Nikolay Patrushev said on Tuesday that Polish statehood could cease to exist within two or three days if Poland entered into a military conflict with Russia. Commenting on Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski's statement that his nation could defeat Russia quickly in the event of a military conflict between the two countries, in an interview with the Russian newspaper Argumenty i Fakty, Patrushev said Russia was not using its full military potential in the conflict in Ukraine. “Speaking about Poland’s military superiority over Russia, Sikorski apparently does not realize that if Poland engages in military action against Russia, our country will use the entire arsenal of forces and means at its disposal, and Polish statehood will cease to exist within two or three days,” he said. Patrushev's remarks came after Sikorski said at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv that Poland and its allies would quickly defeat Russia in the event of a Russian attack. “If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly,” Sikorski said. “We have an undisputed advantage over Russia in terms of air power.” Sikorski later clarified that he had been referring to a potential conflict between NATO and Russia, rather than one between Poland alone and Russia. https://ksevradio.com/exclusive-french-s.text: Advertisement FROM SRN NEWS Exclusive-French supercomputer maker Bull doubles output to boost Europe’s AI ambitions October 1, 2026 SRN News SHARE Share / Copy Link X Facebook By Leo Marchandon Oct 1 (Reuters) – Bull, the state-owned French maker of Europe’s fastest supercomputers, reopened an expanded factory on Thursday to double its production capacity, executives told Reuters, as Europe bolsters its AI computing capacity. The European Union has committed €7 billion ($7.87 billion) over 2021-2027 to a network of supercomputers, aiming to close a compute gap with the United States and China. Bull’s plant in Angers, France, is the only factory in Europe dedicated to building these machines, and its expansion is meant to support that goal. Chief Executive Emmanuel Le Roux said Bull has received more orders this year than ever before, and has won 15 of the 18 tenders issued by EuroHPC, the EU body that co-funds Europe’s network of supercomputers with member states, competing against companies including Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Airbus inaugurated Bull-built supercomputers in Toulouse and Hamburg this year, in a five-year deal worth close to €100 million that tripled the planemaker’s simulation capacity. Cloud operator OVHcloud and European Commission-backed Domyn are both attempting to train frontier-class AI models on Bull’s JUPITER supercomputer alongside other companies Bull declined to name. OUTPUT COULD EXPAND AGAIN IN 2027 The Angers expansion cost €80 million, Bull executives said. Output has already doubled, from six racks a month previously to 12 now, and the plant can boost output to 24 next year on demand it expects to keep growing. France’s order from Bull, a supercomputer named after computer scientist Alice Recoque, accounts for 94 racks, and is being assembled in parallel with LUMI-AI, Finland’s €388 million system and Bull’s biggest-ever contract. The two orders could not have been built alongside each other before the expansion, executives said. France completed its purchase of Bull from debt-laden IT group Atos on March 31, valuing the company at up to €404 million. The original motive was strategic, Le Roux said. In the 1980s, after the United States stopped shipping supercomputers to the CEA, France’s nuclear agency, France turned to Bull to build the machines that were used to simulate nuclear tests. Bull built JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale machine, the fastest class of supercomputers, now running at the Juelich centre in Germany. Alice Recoque, ordered for the CEA, is due for delivery in stages from the end of this year, at a cost of €554 million to the French government and European Union. The Angers factory assembles systems using Nvidia, AMD and Intel processors, or European parts, depending on customer demands. European-made components account for 70% of the machines being built, up from 20% to 30% five years ago. Under a partnership signed in June, Bull and Taiwan’s Foxconn <2317. TW> will also manufacture Nvidia’s NVL systems at a plant in the Czech Republic, with final assembly in the Angers factory.
